To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
ethanol attenuates increases in noradrenaine release in the amyglada and locus coeruleu induced by stress, and increases dopamine release in the accumbens induced by ethanol.

ethanol, in part by its anxiolytic effect, might be involved in the maintenance of ethanol drinking, and that ethanol might have reinforcing effects by enhancing dopamine release in the brain regions related to reward.

stress increases noradrenaline, dopamine and serotonin release in various brain regions, wherein noradrenaline is increased in the amygdalo-locus coeruleus system in response to psychological stress and ethanol attenuates the stress-induced increases in the noradrenaline and dopamine release in the amydgalo-locus system, but not in other brain regions.
In summary, our research is concerned with

the interaction of stress factors with ethanol, and suggests that ethanol might be a kind of stress-reducing agent, at least, by attenuating noradrenaline responses in the amygdaloid and locus coeruleal regions.
the interaction of stress, anxiety and alcohol, which might provide the neurochemical basis for understanding the interaction of stress with alcohol.
the neurobiological mechanisms of interaction of stress and alcohol.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
ethanol ingestion and response are enhanced by various stresses.
the stress-induced increases in the neurotransmission are attenuated by ethanol, but ethanol itself increases the neurotransmission, especially in the mesolimbic system.
stress and ethanol have a bidirectional interaction, and this interaction may be involved in the mechanism for the motivation of drinking ethanol.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
ethanol might have a potential to reduce anxiety and/or fear through the attenuation of stress-induced increases in catecholamine release in the amygdaa, hypothalamus and locus coeruleu.
the interaction of stress with ethanol ingestion and response might be mediated by stress-induced increases in neurotransmitter release in brain regions such as the amygdala.

stress and ethanol interact in the central noradrenergic system and the interaction might be related to the motivation for repeated drinking of ethanol and to the attenuation of stress-induced anxiety.
The main takeaway from our work is that
ethanol, in some brain regions, attenuates stress-induced increases in the release of noradrenaline.

the stress-induced increase in neurotransmitter release, in the extended brain region, might be a common mechanism for stress-induced ethanol intake and that the stress-induced increases in neurotransmitter release in the amygadala and locus coereleus, in part, might be a neurochemical mechanism for the reduction of anxiety and/or tension by ethanol.
the interaction of ethanol with psychological or emotional stress is more important than that of physical stress.
